title: Operating Kubernetes
subtitle: Troubleshooting, access control, Helm, scaling and production readiness
description: Run Kubernetes day to day: diagnose failing pods, grant least-privilege access, package with Helm, scale automatically, maintain nodes safely and harden workloads for production.
outcomes: Diagnose Pending, CrashLoopBackOff, ImagePullBackOff and OOMKilled pods
Design RBAC with ServiceAccounts and verify it with kubectl auth can-i
Deploy, upgrade and roll back with Helm and autoscale with HPA
Drain nodes safely and apply a production hardening checklist

modules.title: Troubleshooting and access
modules.summary: Find failures fast and control who can do what.

lessons.title: Troubleshooting pods
lessons.summary: Read pod status, events and logs to diagnose Pending, CrashLoopBackOff, ImagePullBackOff and OOMKilled.
objectives: Map a pod status to the stage where it failed
Use describe, events and logs --previous to find the cause

sections.title: Start from the status, then ask the right question
sections.body:
Most pod problems fall into a few buckets, and the `STATUS` column of `kubectl get pods` tells you which one. **Pending** means the scheduler has not placed the pod (or it is waiting for a volume). **ImagePullBackOff** / **ErrImagePull** means the kubelet cannot fetch the image. **CrashLoopBackOff** means the container starts, exits, and kubelet is backing off between restarts. **OOMKilled** means the kernel killed the container for exceeding its memory limit.

The workflow is always the same: `get` for the status, `describe` for events and state, `logs` for what the application said.

sections.title: Status to likely cause
head: Status
Typical cause
First command
rows: No node fits the requests, taints, unbound PVC
Wrong tag, private registry without pull secret
App crashes, bad command, failing config

sections.code:
kubectl get pods -o wide
kubectl describe pod web-7d9c8b6f5-abcde
kubectl logs web-7d9c8b6f5-abcde
kubectl logs web-7d9c8b6f5-abcde --previous
kubectl logs web-7d9c8b6f5-abcde -c sidecar
kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp
kubectl get events --field-selector involvedObject.name=web-7d9c8b6f5-abcde
sections.title: The core diagnostic loop
sections.note: `--previous` shows the log of the last terminated container, which is the one that actually crashed. The current container in CrashLoopBackOff often has no output yet.

sections.title: Events expire
sections.body: Events are kept for about an hour by default. If you are investigating an old incident, `describe` may show nothing; check your logging and monitoring stack instead.

sections.code:
kubectl describe pod api-5c7d | sed -n '/Last State/,/Ready/p'
# Last State:  Terminated
#   Reason:    OOMKilled
#   Exit Code: 137

kubectl get pod api-5c7d -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].lastState.terminated.reason}'
sections.title: Confirming an OOM kill
sections.note: Exit code 137 is 128 + 9 (SIGKILL). Raise `resources.limits.memory` or fix the leak; do not just restart.

sections.title: Do not debug by deleting
sections.body: Deleting a crashing pod replaces it with an identical one and destroys the `--previous` logs. Collect evidence first, then act.

exercises.title: Reproduce a CrashLoopBackOff
exercises.prompt: Run a pod that exits immediately, then read why it keeps restarting.
exercises.command: kubectl run crasher --image=busybox --restart=Always -- sh -c 'echo boom; exit 1'
exercises.expected: The pod enters CrashLoopBackOff and `kubectl logs crasher --previous` prints boom.
exercises.hint: Use --previous to see the terminated container's output.

exercises.title: Trigger ImagePullBackOff
exercises.prompt: Create a deployment with a non-existent image tag and find the pull error in the events.
exercises.expected: describe pod shows Failed to pull image ... not found, and status ImagePullBackOff.
exercises.hint: The error is in the Events section at the bottom of describe.

questions.question: You see CrashLoopBackOff. Which command shows why the last attempt died?
questions.explain: --previous prints the log of the terminated container instance that crashed.

questions.question: A pod stays Pending and describe says '0/3 nodes are available: insufficient memory'. What is wrong?
questions.explain: The scheduler cannot find a node with enough allocatable memory for the requests.

questions.question: Which exit code usually accompanies OOMKilled?
questions.explain: 137 = 128 + SIGKILL(9), sent by the kernel OOM killer.

questions.question: Where does kubectl describe show scheduling and image pull failures?
questions.explain: Events record scheduler, kubelet and pull decisions in time order.

lessons.title: RBAC and ServiceAccounts
lessons.summary: Grant least-privilege access with ServiceAccounts, Roles, RoleBindings and ClusterRoles, and verify it with kubectl auth can-i.
objectives: Explain subjects, verbs, resources and bindings
Create a namespaced Role and bind it to a ServiceAccount
Verify and debug permissions with kubectl auth can-i

sections.title: Who can do what, where
sections.body:
**RBAC** is additive: there are no deny rules. A **Role** lists allowed `verbs` on `resources` within one namespace. A **ClusterRole** does the same cluster-wide, or for cluster-scoped objects such as nodes. A **RoleBinding** attaches a Role (or ClusterRole) to subjects inside a namespace; a **ClusterRoleBinding** grants it across the whole cluster.

Pods authenticate to the API server as a **ServiceAccount**. Every namespace has a `default` one; give each workload its own so permissions stay minimal.

sections.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: pod-reader
  namespace: demo
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: pod-reader
  namespace: demo
rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["pods", "pods/log"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: pod-reader
  namespace: demo
subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: pod-reader
    namespace: demo
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: pod-reader
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
sections.title: Read-only access to pods in one namespace
sections.note: `roleRef` is immutable: to change it, delete and recreate the binding.

sections.code:
kubectl auth can-i list pods -n demo --as=system:serviceaccount:demo:pod-reader
kubectl auth can-i delete pods -n demo --as=system:serviceaccount:demo:pod-reader
kubectl auth can-i --list -n demo --as=system:serviceaccount:demo:pod-reader
kubectl get rolebindings,clusterrolebindings -A | grep pod-reader
sections.title: Verify with impersonation
sections.note: Impersonation with `--as` needs permission itself, so run it as an admin. The service account form is `system:serviceaccount:NAMESPACE:NAME`.

sections.title: Avoid cluster-admin shortcuts
sections.body: Binding `cluster-admin` to a workload to make a Forbidden error go away gives that pod full control of the cluster. Read the error, which names the verb and resource, and grant exactly that.

sections.title: Imperative shortcuts
sections.body: `kubectl create role` and `kubectl create rolebinding --dry-run=client -o yaml` generate correct manifests quickly.

exercises.title: Create and test a Role
exercises.prompt: Create a role allowing get/list on pods, bind it to a service account and check it.
exercises.expected: can-i get pods as the service account returns yes; can-i delete pods returns no.
exercises.hint: Use kubectl create role and kubectl create rolebinding --serviceaccount=default:viewer.
exercises.solution:
kubectl create role pod-get --verb=get,list --resource=pods
kubectl create rolebinding viewer-pods --role=pod-get --serviceaccount=default:viewer
kubectl auth can-i get pods --as=system:serviceaccount:default:viewer

exercises.title: List effective permissions
exercises.prompt: Show everything the service account may do in the namespace.
exercises.expected: A table of resources and verbs including pods get/list.

questions.question: What does a RoleBinding do?
options: Grants a Role's permissions to subjects in a namespace
questions.explain: Roles define permissions; bindings attach them to users, groups or service accounts.

questions.question: Can RBAC express an explicit deny?
questions.explain: RBAC only grants; absence of a rule means denied.

questions.question: Which command checks if a service account can list pods in demo?
options: kubectl auth can-i list pods -n demo --as=system:serviceaccount:demo:NAME
questions.explain: auth can-i with --as impersonates the subject.

questions.question: Which object is needed to grant access to nodes?
questions.explain: Nodes are cluster-scoped, so a ClusterRole is required.

lessons.title: Helm basics
lessons.summary: Install, configure, upgrade and roll back applications packaged as Helm charts.
objectives: Install and override values with --set and -f
Upgrade and roll back a release using revision history

sections.title: Charts, values, releases
sections.body:
A **chart** is a package of templated Kubernetes manifests. **Values** (`values.yaml`) are the inputs to those templates. A **release** is one installed instance of a chart in a namespace; Helm stores each revision of it as a Secret, which is what makes rollback possible.

Prefer `helm upgrade --install`, which is idempotent and works in CI whether or not the release exists.

sections.code:
helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
helm repo update
helm search repo nginx
helm show values bitnami/nginx > values-default.yaml
helm install web bitnami/nginx -n demo --create-namespace --set replicaCount=2
helm list -n demo
helm status web -n demo
sections.title: Find and install a chart

sections.code:
replicaCount: 3
service:
  type: ClusterIP
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 100m
    memory: 128Mi
  limits:
    memory: 256Mi
sections.title: my-values.yaml
sections.note: Keep overrides in a file under version control rather than long --set chains.

sections.code:
helm template web bitnami/nginx -f my-values.yaml | less
helm upgrade --install web bitnami/nginx -n demo -f my-values.yaml --atomic --wait
helm history web -n demo
helm rollback web 1 -n demo
helm uninstall web -n demo
sections.title: Render, upgrade, roll back
sections.note: `--atomic` rolls back automatically if the upgrade does not become ready. `helm template` renders locally without touching the cluster.

sections.title: Rollback creates a new revision
sections.body: `helm rollback web 1` does not rewind history: it creates revision N+1 with the contents of revision 1. Persistent data and externally changed state are not reverted.

sections.title: Pin chart versions
sections.body: Without `--version`, an upgrade may pull a newer chart with breaking changes. Pin versions in CI.

exercises.title: Install with overrides
exercises.prompt: Install a chart with a values override and confirm the replica count.
exercises.expected: helm list shows the release deployed and kubectl get deploy web-nginx shows 2/2.
exercises.hint: If the repo is missing, run helm repo add first.
exercises.solution:
helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
helm install web bitnami/nginx --set replicaCount=2
kubectl get deploy

exercises.title: Upgrade and roll back
exercises.prompt: Change replicaCount, inspect history, then return to revision 1.
exercises.expected: helm history shows revisions; after rollback the deployment returns to 2 replicas.
exercises.solution:
helm history web
helm rollback web 1

questions.question: What is a Helm release?
options: An installed instance of a chart
questions.explain: A release is a named, versioned installation of a chart.

questions.question: Which command installs or upgrades idempotently?
questions.explain: upgrade --install creates the release if absent, otherwise upgrades.

questions.question: What does helm template do?
questions.explain: It outputs the rendered YAML, useful for review and diffing.

questions.question: After helm rollback web 1, the history has...
questions.explain: Rollback records a new revision based on the old one.

lessons.title: Autoscaling and node maintenance
lessons.summary: Scale on demand with the HorizontalPodAutoscaler, then safely take nodes out of service with cordon, drain and taints.
objectives: Configure an HPA and understand why requests are required
Cordon and drain a node safely
Use taints and tolerations to steer scheduling

sections.title: Horizontal Pod Autoscaling
sections.body: The **HorizontalPodAutoscaler** adjusts a Deployment's replica count based on observed metrics. CPU utilisation is calculated as a percentage of the pod's **CPU request**, so pods without `resources.requests.cpu` cannot be scaled on CPU. HPA needs **metrics-server** installed to supply resource metrics; `kubectl top` uses the same source.

sections.code:
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: web
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 10
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 70
sections.title: HPA targeting 70% CPU
sections.note: Imperative form: kubectl autoscale deployment web --min=2 --max=10 --cpu-percent=70

sections.code:
kubectl top nodes
kubectl top pods
kubectl get hpa web -w
kubectl describe hpa web
sections.title: Observe scaling
sections.note: If TARGETS shows <unknown>, metrics-server is missing or the pods have no CPU request.

sections.title: Node maintenance
sections.body: To patch or replace a node: **cordon** marks it unschedulable without touching running pods; **drain** cordons and then evicts pods so controllers recreate them elsewhere. Eviction respects PodDisruptionBudgets. **Taints** on a node repel pods unless they carry a matching **toleration**.

sections.code:
kubectl cordon worker-2
kubectl drain worker-2 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
# ... patch, reboot ...
kubectl uncordon worker-2

kubectl taint nodes worker-3 dedicated=gpu:NoSchedule
kubectl taint nodes worker-3 dedicated=gpu:NoSchedule-
sections.title: Cordon, drain, taint
sections.note: The trailing `-` removes a taint. Effects: NoSchedule, PreferNoSchedule, NoExecute (also evicts running pods).

sections.title: Drain needs replicas
sections.body: Draining a node that hosts the only replica of a workload causes downtime. Run at least two replicas and a PodDisruptionBudget first.

exercises.title: Autoscale a deployment
exercises.prompt: Create an HPA for a deployment with min 2, max 5, 60% CPU.
exercises.expected: kubectl get hpa shows web with MINPODS 2 and MAXPODS 5.
exercises.hint: The deployment must define a CPU request.

exercises.title: Cordon a node
exercises.prompt: Mark a node unschedulable and check its status.
exercises.expected: kubectl get nodes shows Ready,SchedulingDisabled; kubectl uncordon NODE restores it.

questions.question: Why must pods set CPU requests for CPU-based HPA?
options: Utilisation is computed relative to the request
questions.explain: Percentage utilisation is current usage divided by the requested CPU.

questions.question: What does kubectl drain do beyond cordon?
questions.explain: Drain cordons and then evicts the pods, honouring PDBs.

questions.question: Why does drain often need --ignore-daemonsets?
options: DaemonSet pods cannot be evicted usefully; they are recreated on the node
questions.explain: DaemonSet pods are tied to every node, so drain refuses unless told to skip them.

questions.question: Which taint effect also evicts already running pods?
questions.explain: NoExecute evicts pods that do not tolerate the taint.

lessons.title: Production checklist
lessons.summary: Harden and prepare a workload: security context, Pod Security, PodDisruptionBudgets, resource policy and observability.
objectives: Use Pod Security Admission labels and PDBs
Set resource policy and probes for observability

sections.title: What production-ready means
sections.body: A workload is production-ready when it fails safely, is limited in what it can do, and can be observed. The checklist: run as **non-root** with a read-only filesystem and dropped capabilities; enforce **Pod Security Standards** per namespace; set **requests and limits**; add **readiness/liveness probes**; protect availability with a **PodDisruptionBudget**; and ship logs and metrics.

sections.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels: {app: api}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: {app: api}
    spec:
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
        seccompProfile: {type: RuntimeDefault}
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: registry.example.com/api:1.4.2
          securityContext:
            allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
            readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
            capabilities: {drop: ["ALL"]}
          resources:
            requests: {cpu: 200m, memory: 256Mi}
            limits: {memory: 256Mi}
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: {path: /healthz, port: 8080}
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet: {path: /livez, port: 8080}
            initialDelaySeconds: 10
sections.title: Hardened Deployment
sections.note: Pin image tags to versions or digests; never use :latest in production.

sections.code:
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  minAvailable: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels: {app: api}
sections.title: PodDisruptionBudget
sections.note: Voluntary disruptions such as drain will not evict below minAvailable.

sections.code:
kubectl label namespace prod pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted
kubectl get pdb
kubectl top pods -n prod
kubectl get events -n prod --sort-by=.lastTimestamp
sections.title: Pod Security Admission and checks
sections.note: Start with `warn` and `audit` modes to see what would break before using `enforce`.

sections.title: Checklist
head: Area
Practice
rows: Non-root, no privilege escalation, drop ALL capabilities, RuntimeDefault seccomp
Requests on everything; memory limit equal to request
3+ replicas, PDB, probes, anti-affinity or topology spread
Structured stdout logs, metrics scraping, alerts on restarts and OOMs

sections.title: CPU limits are debated
sections.body: Memory limits are essential because memory is not compressible. CPU limits can cause throttling; many teams set CPU requests only.

exercises.title: Apply Pod Security labels
exercises.prompt: Label a namespace to warn on restricted violations and then try to run a root pod.
exercises.expected: kubectl run root-test --image=nginx prints a warning listing violated restricted policy fields.
exercises.hint: The namespace label controls the mode: enforce, audit or warn.

exercises.title: Create a PDB
exercises.prompt: Create a PDB for deployment web keeping at least 1 pod available.
exercises.expected: kubectl get pdb shows ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS based on the replica count.

questions.question: What does a PodDisruptionBudget protect against?
questions.explain: PDBs limit evictions caused by voluntary operations; they cannot stop hardware failure.

questions.question: Which securityContext setting prevents a process from gaining more privileges than its parent?
questions.explain: allowPrivilegeEscalation: false sets no_new_privs on the container.

questions.question: Which Pod Security Standards level is the most restrictive?
questions.explain: The levels are privileged, baseline and restricted.

questions.question: Why start Pod Security rollout with warn mode?
options: To see violations without blocking pods
questions.explain: warn and audit report violations while still admitting pods.
